P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. As an EU member state, Latvia applies Article 63 TFEU, which prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments between EU countries and with non-EU countries. Banks still apply AML/KYC checks and may ask for the source of funds.

P2_fcy_account.answer: Very likely yes: Article 63 TFEU removes capital-movement restrictions, and EU banks and e-money institutions commonly offer foreign-currency or multi-currency accounts. No Latvia-specific source on account rules was captured.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: A self-employed person (saimnieciskās darbības veicējs) registers with the State Revenue Service (VID) through its Electronic Declaration System (EDS), using their personal ID code. You give a main NACE 2 activity code and choose a regime: the general regime (social contributions quarterly, income tax annually, expenses deductible) or the micro-enterprise tax (MUN, see L7).

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Tax residents of Latvia are taxed on worldwide income (see quoted rules for exceptions such as remittance-basis regimes). 25.5% up to EUR 105,300; 33% above. Inference (general source principle, not quoted): work performed while living in Latvia for foreign clients is normally taxable in Latvia. 2026 parameters: personal income tax (IIN) is 25.5% up to EUR 105,300 a year and 33% above, plus 3% on total annual income above EUR 200,000. The non-taxable minimum is EUR 550 a month (EUR 570 in 2027). Under the general regime, the self-employed minimum contribution (VSAOI) base is EUR 780 a month in 2026.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: National threshold: VAT registration at EUR 50,000 of taxable transactions in the previous 12 months. Certain non-taxable transactions (real estate, financial and insurance services) also count. From 2025, a person exceeding the threshold by no more than 10% in the year can stay unregistered until the year-end. Cross-border services: a self-employed person supplying cross-border services must register from the first such transaction (practitioner source). The standard VAT rate is 21%. Under the EU SME scheme, small businesses below a national threshold (at most EUR 85,000) can be exempt on domestic sales. Where services are taxed (EU-wide rules, illustrated by Irish Revenue guidance): (1) B2B, meaning services to business customers in other EU countries or outside the EU, are taxed where the customer is established, so no Latvia VAT is charged; EU business customers self-account under the reverse charge. (2) B2C services to private individuals are, as a rule, taxed where the supplier is established, so Latvia VAT applies once you are VAT-registered. (3) Exception: consultancy, legal, accounting, engineering, data-processing, advertising, licensing and electronically supplied services to private customers outside the EU are outside EU VAT, subject to 'use and enjoyment' rules. Electronically supplied services to private customers in other EU countries follow special OSS rules (not captured here).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies directly in Latvia, supervised by the national data protection authority. It covers EU businesses and non-EU businesses offering goods or services to people in the EU.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: EU consumer law gives a 14-day withdrawal right for online and distance purchases without justification: 14 days from delivery for goods, and from conclusion of the contract for services. Exceptions include personalised goods, perishables and date-specific services.

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: For goods this means 14 days from the date of delivery, for services 14 days after the day the contract was agreed.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: Micro-enterprise tax (MUN): a single 25% tax on turnover replaces social contributions and income tax for the owner. Expenses are not deductible, and VAT payers cannot use it. The turnover cap is reported as EUR 50,000 (TaxRavens) but EUR 40,000 in another 2026 guide; unresolved. From 1 April 2027 (adopted 17 September 2026), a beginner micro-enterprise tax of 10% of turnover applies to small side activity. Conditions: sales only to private individuals, turnover up to EUR 12,000 a year, not VAT-registered, no employees, receipts through a special business-income account. TRAP: B2B freelancers can't use the 10% regime, and it builds no social insurance.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
